ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the figure shows a common-collector (emitter follower) NPN transistor circuit. The transistor's collector is directly connected to the +15 V power supply; the base is driven by the input source on the left labeled Vin, and the lower end of the input source is grounded; the emitter is the output node on the right labeled Vout, and this output node is connected to ground through a 1.5 kΩ resistor. Then reason: the problem gives the input voltage Vin = 0.0 V, and the base-emitter forward voltage drop of a silicon NPN transistor is about 0.7 V. When a common-collector circuit conducts, usually Vout ≈ Vin - 0.7 V. Substituting gives 0.0 - 0.7 = -0.7 V. But this circuit has no negative power supply, and the output node is grounded through a resistor, so the output cannot be pulled to a negative voltage; when Vin = 0.0 V, the base-emitter junction cannot be forward-conducting, the transistor is cut off, and the output node is held at ground potential by the 1.5 kΩ resistor. Therefore the output voltage is 0 V.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the collector at +15 V, the base input Vin, and the emitter/output node feeding a 1.5 kΩ resistor to ground. From the text, take Vin = 0.0 V and VBE ≈ 0.7 V. Apply the common-collector rule Vout ≈ max(0, Vin - 0.7 V). Since 0.0 - 0.7 = -0.7 V is below ground and the load is grounded with no negative supply, the transistor is cut off and the output remains at 0 V.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: note that Vout is the emitter node and is tied to ground through the 1.5 kΩ resistor, while the base is held at Vin. From the text, set the base voltage to 0.0 V. Test whether the transistor can be on: an on silicon NPN would require Ve = Vb - 0.7 = -0.7 V. That would put the output node below ground even though the only connection from that node besides the transistor is a resistor to ground, and the NPN emitter follower cannot source a negative voltage in this circuit. Therefore the assumed on state is invalid; the transistor is cut off. With the transistor off, the 1.5 kΩ resistor fixes Vout at ground, so Vout = 0 V.
